title: Kasoli nu Saak
localName: Kasoli nu Saak — Kasoli ane Jugu nu Saak
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Gram flour cooked in oil to pinkish-brown, ground peanuts stirred in for five minutes more, then yoghurt and spices off the heat and corn cobs returned in six hundred millilitres of their own cooking water.
longDesc: Kasoli nu saak is the Indian-Ugandan dish in its clearest form, and the name says so: kasoli is Swahili for sweetcorn, saak is Gujarati for curry. A Swahili noun inside a Gujarati grammatical frame. This version is documented from the inside — an old Gujarati preparation of corn in chickpea flour and yoghurt, amended by the author's grandmother to include peanuts after her years living in Uganda. That is hybridity attested by the family it happened to, not inferred.
ingredients: 875 g fresh or frozen corn cobs (about 4), halved
50 g gram flour (chickpea or besan flour)
45 ml (3 tbsp) fresh coriander, finely chopped
// Plus about 600 ml of the corn's own cooking water
steps: Boil salted water and add the corn — 6 to 8 minutes if frozen, 5 if fresh — then let it rest. Reserve the cooking water.
Heat the oil, add the gram flour and stir continuously 4 to 5 minutes until pinkish-brown.
Add the ground peanuts and stir another five minutes.
Remove from the heat and mix in the yoghurt, salt, turmeric, chilli powder and sugar.
Add the sweetcorn and return to medium heat.
Slowly add about 600 ml of the reserved cooking water while stirring.
Cover and heat through 5 minutes, until the sauce is the consistency of double cream.
Garnish with the coriander. Serve with rice, chapatis, or on its own.
chefTips: Reserve the corn water. Six hundred millilitres of it goes back into the sauce, and that is where the sweetcorn flavour ends up.
Cook the gram flour to pinkish-brown, four to five minutes of continuous stirring. Under-cooked gram flour tastes raw and chalky and it is the commonest fault in this dish.
Add the yoghurt off the heat. On the heat it will split, every time.
Double cream is the consistency to aim for. Thinner and it slides off the corn; thicker and it claggs.
This is a rarity among Indian dishes in having no onions, no ginger and no garlic. Do not add them.
The peanuts are the Ugandan addition. The Gujarati original was corn in chickpea flour and a yoghurt sauce, and the peanuts came in after the author's grandmother's years in Uganda.

A second quantified version of the same dish builds it on tomato and onion instead of yoghurt — three-quarters of a cup of tomato puree, pureed onion and garlic, and a green chilli-ginger paste, with the peanuts powdered and 500 ml of water. That is a genuine divergence in the tradition rather than one version being wrong, and it is worth knowing both exist.
The fuller name is Kasoli ane Jugu nu Saak, jugu being the peanut element, which is useful if you are looking it up.
commonMistakes: Letting the sauce reduce past double cream.
sources: Adapted from Meera Sodha, 'Gujarati corn-on-the-cob in a yoghurt and peanut sauce', meerasodha.wordpress.com, 7 April 2014 — all quantities, the 6-to-8-minute or 5-minute corn boil, the reserve-the-cooking-water instruction, the 4-to-5-minute gram flour roux to pinkish-brown, the further five minutes with the ground peanuts, the off-the-heat yoghurt and spices, the roughly 600 ml of reserved water and the double-cream consistency are all hers.

Her headnote is the provenance: the dish came from her grandmother's recipe collection, is an old Gujarati preparation traditionally made with chickpea flour and a yoghurt sauce, and was amended to include peanuts after her grandmother's many years living in Uganda. She also notes it is a rarity among Indian dishes in having no onions, ginger or garlic. Sodha's great-grandfather moved from Gujarat to Uganda in 1913 and her grandfather followed in the 1940s.

The etymology — kasoli meaning sweetcorn in Swahili and saak meaning curry in Gujarati — is from Evie Raja, 'Ugandan-Asian Food and Identity 50 Years On', The Isis Magazine, 11 December 2022, which gives no quantities and is cited for the naming argument only.

The tomato-and-onion version, and the fuller name Kasoli ane Jugu nu Saak, are from Hayley Dhanecha's 'Sweetcorn and Peanut Curry (Kasoli Nu Saak)' at Jagruti's Cooking Odyssey, whose own headnote calls it an East African recipe made by Gujarati Indians who grew up in East Africa. That recipe calls for mustard seeds in its method without listing them, and gives no quantity for them anywhere.

Yasmin Alibhai-Brown's 'The Settler's Cookbook' (Granta, 2008) is the one Ugandan-Asian cookbook and could not be retrieved: the Internet Archive's search-inside is an XHR widget and returned no page text or snippets. That gap is real.
reheating: Warm gently. Do not boil, or the yoghurt will split.
healthBenefits: Gram flour and peanuts together give a substantial amount of plant protein.
Yoghurt adds calcium, protein and live cultures.
Sweetcorn supplies fibre, folate and the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin.
culturalNote: The Gujarati trading community arrived with the Uganda Railway and its dukas were the commercial spine of the colonial economy. Idi Amin announced the expulsion on 4 August 1972 and extended it on 9 August, with a ninety-day ultimatum expiring in early November; the first evacuation flight landed at Stansted on 18 September. Estimates of those affected range from 55,000 to 80,000 and cannot be reconciled from the published sources. This dish went with them, which is why the recipe survives in Lincolnshire and the name survives in two languages.
